title: Galactic refurbishment
caption: The emission line galaxy UGC 5797, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The smudge of stars at the centre is UGC 5797, an emission line galaxy, which means it is actively forming stars. As massive, bright blue stars are born, its stellar population is constantly being renewed. Galaxies with lots of star formation often take on a blue tint and keep the cycle of stellar birth going.
Behind UGC 5797 lies a scattering of spiral galaxies. Spirals are rich in dust and gas, the raw material for stars, so they often count as emission line galaxies too.

The background spirals also show how much a galaxy's look depends on the angle we see it from. Their discs can appear very different. Some here face us, revealing the structure of their spiral arms, while the two at bottom left are seen edge-on and look like plain streaks. Many others, in a range of colours and at different tilts, are sprinkled across the frame.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the field in visible and near-infrared light at 606 nm and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, revealing faint background spirals.

explore: Luca Limatola entered a version of this image in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition. The Hubble data come from the Advanced Camera for Surveys, using one visible and one near-infrared filter.
alt: A faint smudge of stars at the centre, surrounded by spiral galaxies at various angles, including two thin edge-on streaks at lower left.
